title: Quantification of Medical Waste and Incineration‐Related CO2 Emissions Associated With Gastrointestinal Endoscopy at Two Facilities in Japan: A Preliminary Observational Study

esophagogastroduodenoscopy
endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
endoscopic submucosal dissection
gastrointestinal endoscopy.

Climate change increasingly threatens global health. Paradoxically, healthcare also contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions through energy consumption, transportation, and the generation of medical waste [1]. Japan, with a rapidly aging population, has had difficulty maintaining a sustainable healthcare system, and its government has set targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 46% from 2013 levels by 2030 and to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050 [2].

Gastrointestinal endoscopy (GIE), one of the most frequently performed examinations at healthcare facilities, represents the third largest source of hospital‐activity‐related medical waste [3]; disposable devices are widely used in GIE to maintain sterility and safety [4]. However, the high daily volume of procedures (e.g., esophagogastroduodenoscopy [EGD] and colonoscopy [CS]) means that the cumulative environmental burden of GIE is considerable. Therefore, “green endoscopy” was introduced by the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy and other organizations to promote environmentally sustainable endoscopic practices through initiatives such as carbon footprint assessment, waste reduction, and workflow optimization [5].

Green endoscopy is broadly supported by endoscopy staff in the Asia–Pacific region but is rarely implemented in practice [6]. Despite the increased frequency of GIE procedures, few studies have quantitatively evaluated the characteristics and extent of GIE‐generated medical waste [7], particularly in East Asian countries, including Japan. Accordingly, to identify methods to improve sustainability in clinical practice, we quantify the medical waste generated from routine upper and lower GIE procedures in Japan and subsequently estimate the associated incineration‐related CO2 emissions to provide preliminary baseline data to support more environmentally sustainable endoscopy practices.

Surveys were undertaken between June 2024 and January 2025 at a secondary medical institution (Kagawa Rosai Hospital) and a university hospital (Kagawa University Hospital) in Japan. A total of 137 GIEs were audited: 131 at Kagawa Rosai Hospital (79 EGDs, 38 CSs, 10 endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatographies [ERCPs], and four endoscopic submucosal dissections [ESDs]) and six ESDs at Kagawa University Hospital, making ESDs the only type of procedure measured at both institutions.

All the procedures were performed by a single operator (Ryosuke Kawanishi), and the disposable devices used were essentially identical; the classification and segregation of the waste, and the subsequent disposal and incineration pathways, were identical at the two institutions. Data from both institutions were, therefore, combined.

For each audited procedure, the duration from the endoscope's insertion to its complete withdrawal was recorded using a digital timer, and the medical waste was weighed on a calibrated electronic scale with a readability of 2 g, at the level of aggregation described in the next paragraph. Waste was categorized as infectious (combustible and non‐combustible), non‐infectious (combustible and non‐combustible), liquid (such as suctioned fluids), and sharps or other materials designated for a landfill. Each category was quantified separately; liquid waste was recorded by volume and converted to mass, assuming a density of 1 g/mL. Infectious waste comprised waste contaminated with patients’ body fluids; non‐infectious waste included packaging materials for medical devices. All the disposable items used or generated during each procedure were collected and weighed (e.g., biopsy forceps, sheaths, snares, knives, syringes, gauze, drapes, and disposal bags). Personal protective equipment used outside the procedure room was not included.

The duration of each procedure was recorded in all four groups, using the same definition throughout. Waste was collected only from the audited procedures—those performed by the first author and for which the procedure duration was measured—and not from other procedures performed in the same room. For ESDs and ERCPs, the waste was weighed separately for each case; for EGDs and CSs, it was pooled and weighed as a single daily total across 16 and 15 measurement days, respectively, so that attribution to individual cases was impossible. Per‐procedure and time‐adjusted values for EGDs and CSs are, therefore, derived from these daily totals.

This study was approved by the Clinical Ethics Committee of Kagawa University Hospital (Registration No. 2025–074) and was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Kagawa Rosai Hospital determined that formal ethics review was not required at that institution (see Ethics Statement).

The total amount of waste was calculated based solely on weight (g), including landfill waste. CO2 emissions were estimated from the per‐endoscopy waste (excluding non‐incinerated liquid and landfill wastes) by modeling waste incineration. This analysis does not represent the complete carbon footprint of each procedure. At both study institutions, both infectious and non‐infectious medical wastes (combustible or otherwise) were incinerated. Accordingly, combustible and non‐combustible wastes were approximated as cellulose (C6H10O5)n and polyethylene (CH2)n, respectively.
CO2 emissions were estimated using the following combustion equations [8]:
(C6H10O5)n + 6nO2 → 6nCO2 + 5nH2O
(CH2)n + 1.5nO2 → nCO2 + nH2O

The waste and estimated CO2 emissions per minute of endoscopy were calculated by dividing the total values by the procedural duration (in minutes), and the annual CO2 emissions by multiplying the aggregate per‐procedure estimates by the annual procedure volumes. Because almost all the measurements were obtained at Kagawa Rosai Hospital, the primary annual estimate was calculated using the annual procedure volume of that institution (2314 EGDs, 1753 CSs, 295 ERCPs, and 21 ESDs).

To evaluate the robustness of the estimated CO2 emissions relative to the chemical approximations used, a scenario‐based sensitivity analysis was performed. The three scenarios were a base composition scenario, using the chemical approximations (where combustible and non‐combustible wastes were approximated as cellulose and polyethylene, respectively); a lower‐emission composition scenario, where all the incineration‐eligible waste was assumed to behave as cellulose; and a higher‐emission composition scenario, where all such waste was assumed to behave as polyethylene. The same combustion equations were applied. Liquid and landfill‐designated wastes were excluded from each scenario.

Importantly, this analysis only addresses the uncertainty in the assumed chemical composition of the incinerated waste. Other sources of uncertainty—including alternative disposal pathways, transport distances, moisture content, combustion efficiency, and energy recovery—were not varied, and the scenarios, therefore, do not represent the overall lower and upper bounds of the uncertainty in the estimated emissions.

All the statistical analyses were performed using JMP Pro v17.0 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). The amounts of waste and per‐procedure and per‐minute CO2 emissions were calculated in MS Excel. Throughout the text and tables, n denotes the total number of procedures and m the number of measurement days.

For each procedure type, the principal per‐procedure and time‐adjusted values are aggregate estimates, calculated as (the total waste mass or total estimated CO2 emissions) divided by (the total number of procedures) or (the total procedure duration in minutes) across all the measurements. These are aggregate ratios and are not means of case‐ or day‐level values.

To describe variability, case‐ and day‐level values were also derived. For ESDs and ERCPs, the waste mass, estimated CO2 emissions, and per‐minute rates were calculated for each case. For EGDs and CSs, the following values were calculated for each measurement day: the daily total waste divided by the number of procedures performed that day, and the daily total waste or estimated CO2 emissions divided by the total procedure duration on that day. The distributions of these case‐ and day‐level values, and the number of procedures performed per measurement day, are summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD) with the observed range. Because case‐level waste data were not available for EGDs and CSs, the distributions reported for both procedures describe the variability across measurement days and do not imply case‐level precision.
No inferential tests or group comparisons were performed because our objective was to provide preliminary descriptive baseline data for environmental impact assessments.

sections.title: Amounts of Waste and Per‐Examination and Per‐Procedure CO2 Emissions

paragraphs.en: On average, EGDs, CSs, ESDs, and ERCPs generated 626, 997, 3406, and 2707 g of waste, respectively. Estimated incineration‐related per‐procedure CO2 emissions (excluding landfill‐designated and liquid wastes) were the highest for ESDs (5834 g), followed by ERCPs, CSs, and EGDs (4780, 1178, and 949 g, respectively). Among the waste categories, non‐combustible infectious waste accounted for the highest mass in both ESDs and ERCPs. The waste designated for landfill disposal (e.g., electrosurgical units and puncture needles) was the highest in ESDs (averaging 308 g per procedure).

A mean of 4.9 ± 1.5 EGDs (range 2–8) and 2.5 ± 1.0 CSs (range 1–5) were performed on each measurement day. Across the 16 EGD measurement days, the amount of day‐level per‐procedure waste was 644 ± 122 g (range 450–847), and the corresponding estimated CO2 emissions were 981 ± 181 g (range 713–1368). Across the 15 CS measurement days, the corresponding values were 1047 ± 297 g (range 766–2018) and 1200 ± 232 g (range 954–1718), respectively. The wide range for CSs reflects a single measurement day on which only one procedure was performed, and 1550 of the 2018 g of waste recorded was liquid.
The quantities of each waste category, including the case‐level distributions for ESDs and ERCPs, are detailed in Table 1. Representative waste from a single ESD is illustrated in Figure 1.

sections.title: Waste and CO2 Emissions Generated Per Unit of Procedure Time

paragraphs.en: When adjusted for procedure duration, the aggregate estimated CO2 emission rate was the highest for ERCPs (168 g/min), followed by EGDs, CSs, and ESDs (165, 89, and 75 g/min, respectively). The corresponding case‐ and day‐level rates were 190.8 ± 87.9 g/min for ERCPs (case level, n = 10; range 82.1–347.4), 183.7 ± 68.8 g/min for EGDs (day level, m = 16; range 125.5–384.4), 106.9 ± 60.3 g/min for ESDs (case level, n = 10; range 28.3–205.1), and 101.1 ± 26.0 g/min for CSs (day level, m = 15; range 49.9–154.8). Although ESDs had the highest per‐procedure CO2 emissions, short‐duration EGDs and ERCPs had the highest per‐minute CO2 emissions. ESDs and CSs were ordered differently by both estimators: ESDs ranked above CSs by the mean case‐ and day‐level rates but below CSs by the aggregate rate, reflecting the wide variation in the ESD duration (28.7–223.1 min), which weights the aggregate rate toward the longest cases. These results are summarized in Table 2.

Applied to the annual procedure volume of Kagawa Rosai Hospital, the estimated annual GIE‐derived incineration‐related CO2 emissions were approximately 2200, 2070, 120, and 1410 kg for EGDs, CSs, ESDs, and ERCPs, respectively, for a total of approximately 5800 kg. Although ESDs generated the highest per‐procedure emissions, the highest annual institutional contributions were derived from EGDs and CSs, reflecting their high procedure volumes.

sections.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Incineration‐Related CO2 Emissions

paragraphs.en: The per‐procedure CO2 emissions varied depending on the assumptions about the waste's chemical composition (Table 3). The estimated emissions were approximately 64%–69% of the base composition scenario values in the lower‐emission composition scenario (where all the incineration‐eligible waste behaved as cellulose) and 123%–134% in the higher‐emission composition scenario (where all such waste behaved as polyethylene). The per‐minute CO2 emissions varied within a similar relative range (49–115 and 94–221 g/min for the lower‐ and higher‐emission composition scenarios, respectively). The relative ranking of the procedures was maintained across scenarios; in each, ESDs had the highest per‐procedure emissions, and ERCPs and EGDs had the highest per‐minute emissions.

These results are the first to quantify medical waste and the associated incineration‐related CO2 emissions for four gastrointestinal endoscopic procedures performed in clinical settings in Japan. ESDs had the highest per‐procedure CO2 emissions, and both ERCPs and EGDs had the highest per‐minute emissions. Our results are particularly relevant to settings where procedures are performed frequently or depend heavily on medical devices.

The proportionally large amount of ESD‐derived landfill waste may reflect the complexity and invasiveness of ESDs. GIEs generate considerable waste, mainly because of their reliance on single‐use devices [4] and because therapeutic procedures are usually more resource‐intensive than diagnostic ones [9]; our finding that ESDs generated the most per‐procedure waste is consistent with these observations. Welsch et al. [9] reported an average of approximately 1.1 kg of waste per procedure and classified per‐procedure waste as low (<0.5 kg), moderate (0.5–1.5 kg), or high (>1.5 kg), with ERCPs in the high category. To the best of our knowledge, the ESD‐generated waste volume in Japan has not been previously evaluated; we report herein that ESDs generate more waste than ERCPs, also placing ESDs in the high category.

The high per‐minute CO2 emissions in ERCPs and EGDs reflect different underlying mechanisms. Because the amount of materials used per EGD is relatively constant and the procedure is fast, the time‐adjusted waste generation rate is high. However, although the procedure time for ERCPs is longer than that of EGDs, the per‐procedure waste volume of ERCPs is higher, producing a similarly high per‐minute waste generation rate. Most previous studies have evaluated the environmental impacts of GIEs per procedure without adjusting for duration, leaving differences in time‐related efficiency unexplored. Our finding that diagnostic EGDs and therapeutic ERCPs generated the highest per‐minute CO2 emissions is new and suggests that even short diagnostic procedures may have considerable time‐adjusted environmental impacts when the per‐case material usage is relatively fixed. Lacroute et al. [10] reported that a single examination emitted 28.4 kg of CO2e (carbon dioxide equivalents). Reported waste quantities vary considerably between settings [11], reaching 3.03 kg per procedure in a prospective audit of a single endoscopy unit [12]. The estimated environmental impact mainly depends on assumptions about system boundaries, waste disposal scenarios, and emission factors [13]. We focus on incineration‐associated CO2 emissions, estimated from measured waste volumes, because at both institutions, medical waste, other than landfill‐designated items, is incinerated.

The volume of per‐endoscopy medical waste varies by country and facility: Menini et al. [14] reported approximately 1.91 kg of regulated waste per procedure in a single Italian center; Rughwani et al. [15] reported 0.504 kg per procedure at a tertiary care facility in India, and Jung et al. [7] reported an average per‐procedure weight of 1.34 kg across multiple hospitals in South Korea (approximately 0.24 and 0.43 kg for an EGD and a CS, respectively). Our per‐procedure waste masses for an EGD and a CS exceed those of Jung et al. [7], possibly because of differences in clinical practice and in the range of disposable items included in the measurement. A direct comparison of CO2 values is also hampered because the South Korean study reported waste masses only, whereas our estimates are derived from incineration modeling. Our time‐adjusted emissions further suggest that both rapid diagnostic procedures with a relatively fixed material usage and longer therapeutic procedures with a high material usage may represent important targets for waste reduction interventions.

This study has several important limitations. First, we estimate CO2 emissions solely from the incineration of the measured waste, using simplified chemical approximations for combustible (cellulose) and non‐combustible (polyethylene) materials, and this does not reflect the overall carbon footprint of each procedure. Because emissions from upstream processes (e.g., the manufacture and transportation of disposable equipment), equipment reprocessing, water and energy consumption, and transport to disposal facilities are not included, the total environmental impact may be underestimated. Second, our sensitivity analysis (Table 3) only addresses the uncertainty in the waste's composition. Other sources of uncertainty, including alternative disposal routes, transport distances, moisture content, combustion efficiency, energy recovery, and emission factors, were not evaluated, and the scenario range should, therefore, not be interpreted as the overall lower and upper bounds of the emission estimates. Third, the numbers of ERCPs and ESDs were limited to 10 each. Because both procedures vary depending on indications, disease characteristics, lesion locations, and the equipment used, our sample size could not adequately capture their variability, limiting the generalizability of our findings. Fourth, because the waste for EGDs and CSs was pooled by day, their reported distributions describe the variability across the 16 and 15 measurement days, respectively, rather than across individual cases; the procedure duration, by contrast, was recorded for every procedure. Fifth, the contributions of the two institutions were markedly unbalanced: 131 of the 137 audited procedures were performed at Kagawa Rosai Hospital, and only six ESDs came from Kagawa University Hospital. The per‐procedure estimates for EGDs, CSs, and ERCPs are, therefore, single‐center values, and multicenter measurements with a more balanced contribution from each institution are needed before these estimates can be generalized.

Given Japan's commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050, any strategy that expands reusable equipment use, optimizes disposable item use, and develops low‐impact alternatives will contribute to this goal. Although our preliminary baseline data can support greener endoscopy and reduce the environmental impact of this sector, future studies applying full life‐cycle assessment frameworks are needed.

This study was approved by the Clinical Ethics Committee of Kagawa University Hospital (Registration No. 2025‐074) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The component conducted at Kagawa Rosai Hospital was referred to that institution, which determined that the study did not fall within the scope of the Japanese Ethical Guidelines for Medical and Biological Research Involving Human Subjects and that a formal ethics review, therefore, was not required there. This determination reflects the fact that the study only recorded the mass of the medical waste generated by each procedure and the duration of each procedure; no patient‐identifiable information, clinical data, or biological specimens were collected, and no intervention was performed. As this study did not involve any intervention or the use of identifiable patient data, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived by the ethics committee, and an opt‐out approach was used in accordance with institutional policy. This study was not prospectively registered in a clinical trial registry because it is an observational study of medical waste rather than a clinical trial. Furthermore, this study did not involve animals and, therefore, did not require approval related to animal experimentation.
